# veld

> Open-source local development environment orchestrator. One command starts every service with real HTTPS URLs — no port numbers, no manual wiring. Works with monorepos, multi-repo setups, or any project directory.

veld is a Rust-based CLI tool that replaces the ritual of opening multiple terminals, remembering ports, and manually wiring services together. You declare your stack in a single `veld.json`, and veld resolves the dependency graph, allocates ports, starts processes, runs health checks, configures Caddy for HTTPS, and gives you clean URLs like `https://frontend.my-feature.myproject.localhost`.

- Source: https://github.com/prosperity-solutions/veld
- Website: https://veld.oss.life.li
- License: MIT
- Platforms: macOS (arm64/x64), Linux (x64/arm64)

---

## Install

```sh
curl -fsSL https://veld.oss.life.li/get | bash
```

This detects your OS and architecture, downloads the latest release, and installs:
- `veld` to `~/.local/bin/`
- `veld-helper` and `veld-daemon` to `~/.local/lib/veld/`

No sudo required. Ensure `~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`.

**Upgrading from an older veld:** `veld.json` must declare `"schemaVersion": "3"`; `"1"` and `"2"` no longer load. The load error names every change needed. See `docs/migrating-to-v3.md` for the complete rule set, then `veld lint` to verify.

Setup is optional — commands auto-bootstrap on first use with HTTPS on port 18443.
For the full experience with clean URLs (no port numbers), run the one-time privileged setup:

```sh
veld setup privileged
```

This registers system services and binds ports 80/443, so your URLs are just
`https://frontend.my-feature.myproject.localhost` — no `:18443` suffix. Requires
sudo once; you won't be asked again.

Alternatively, `veld setup unprivileged` does a no-sudo setup with HTTPS on port 18443.
Both modes support the full feature set with one difference: unprivileged mode uses port 18443 in URLs and only supports `.localhost` domains (RFC 6761). Custom apex domains (e.g. `{service}.mycompany.dev`) require `veld setup privileged` since they need `/etc/hosts` or dnsmasq management.

To install a specific version: `VELD_VERSION=1.0.0 curl -fsSL https://veld.oss.life.li/get | bash`

### Build from source

```sh
git clone https://github.com/prosperity-solutions/veld.git
cd veld
cargo build --release
# Binaries: target/release/veld, target/release/veld-helper, target/release/veld-daemon
```

---

## Quick Start

1. Create a `veld.json` (or `veld.jsonc` — both are read; with both present `veld.json` wins and lint reports it) in your project root:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://veld.oss.life.li/schema/v3/veld.schema.json",
  "schemaVersion": "3",
  "name": "myproject",
  "url_template": "{service}.{run}.{project}.localhost",
  "nodes": {
    "backend": {
      "default_variant": "local",
      "variants": {
        "local": {
          "type": "start_server",
          "shell": "npm run dev -- --port ${veld.port}",
          "health_check": { "type": "http", "path": "/health", "timeout_seconds": 30 }
        }
      }
    },
    "frontend": {
      "default_variant": "local",
      "variants": {
        "local": {
          "type": "start_server",
          "shell": "npm run dev -- --port ${veld.port}",
          "health_check": { "type": "http", "path": "/", "timeout_seconds": 30 },
          "depends_on": { "backend": "local" }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

2. Start the environment:

```sh
veld start frontend:local --name dev
```

`--name` is optional: when omitted, the run name is inferred from the current git worktree folder, then the git branch (slugified), then the project folder, falling back to a random name. Pass `--name` to override.

Veld resolves the dependency graph (backend first, then frontend), allocates ports, starts processes, runs health checks, configures Caddy routes, and gives you HTTPS URLs.

3. Check status:

```sh
veld status --name dev
veld urls --name dev
```

4. Stop:

```sh
veld stop --name dev
```

---

## Config safety properties (schemaVersion 3)

- **`argv` vs `shell`.** `argv` is an array spawned directly with no shell; interpolation runs per
  element *after* the array is fixed, so an interpolated value containing spaces, quotes, or globs
  can never change the argument count. `shell` is a string run via `sh -c` and is permanently
  supported for pipes, `&&`, and redirection.
- **Secrets are a pointer plus a flag, never custody.** A value can be read from `env`, a `file`, or
  the stdout of an `argv`/`shell` command, and marked `secret: true`. veld resolves it at run start
  and passes it via the process environment or a delivered file (and only if the resolved plan
  reaches it, so a credential helper is not run for a service you did not start). A `secret` value
  veld *substitutes* into an `argv` element or `shell` string — `${vars.x}`, `${output.x}`,
  `${nodes.a.x}` — is a lint **error**, because the value lands in the process table for certain. A
  bare `$NAME` is a **warning** instead: the shell expands it, so it leaks only when the expansion
  becomes another program's argument (`PGPASSWORD=$DB_PASS psql …` is safe;
  `psql "postgres://u:$DB_PASS@host/db"` is not — the shell execs psql with the password in its
  argv). `veld config` prints a redacted placeholder and there is no flag that prints a resolved
  secret.
- **`veld lint` reports every semantic problem at once** and exits non-zero, for CI. Covers unknown
  built-in variables, built-ins written where they are not populated (`${veld.url}` on a `command`
  node, `${veld.port}` in a `vars` value), a `${nodes.X}` naming a node that does not exist or one
  a given preset's plan does not contain, unresolvable presets (dangling `@ref`, cycles, unknown
  node or variant), secrets heading for a command line, credential-shaped literals, and
  reserved-but-inert keys. Semantic problems are deliberately *not* load errors, so a config that
  has drifted can still be torn down with `veld stop`.

## CLI Reference

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `veld start [NODE:VARIANT...] --name <n> [-d]` | Start an environment (`-d` for detached). Given nothing to start: prompts with the preset list (enter takes `default_preset`), or without a TTY uses `default_preset` directly |
| `veld start --preset <NAME-OR-KEY>` | Start a preset by name, or by the stable key `veld presets` shows. A bare preset name as a positional does **not** work — positionals are `node:variant` selections |
| `veld start <NODE:VARIANT> --oneshot [--all-logs]` | Run a command node as a one-off: start its dependencies, run it to completion (streaming its output), tear everything down in reverse order, and exit with its exit code. The e2e-test / CI pattern (like `docker compose run --rm --abort-on-container-exit`). Only the terminal node's output goes to stdout unless `--all-logs`. |
| `veld stop [--name <n>] [--all]` | Stop a running environment |
| `veld restart [--name <n>]` | Restart an environment |
| `veld status [--name <n>] [--json]` | Show run status, including per-node CPU and memory usage |
| `veld urls [--name <n>] [--json]` | Show URLs for a run |
| `veld action <name> [--name <n>] [--node <n>] [--print] [--json]` | Run a node-defined action (e.g. open the database in a GUI client); `--print` emits the resolved command |
| `veld actions [--json]` | List the actions defined across the project's nodes |
| `veld logs [--name <n>] [--node <n>] [--lines <n>] [-f] [--since <d>] [--source <s>] [-s <term>] [-C <n>] [--run <id>] [-p] [--all-runs]` | View logs — defaults to the latest run; `--run <id-prefix>` reads a past run, `-p` the previous one, `--all-runs` interleaves everything; `-f` follow (exits when the run ends) |
| `veld graph [NODE:VARIANT...]` | Print dependency graph |
| `veld nodes` | List all nodes and variants |
| `veld presets [--json] [--pin]` | List presets with their keys, labels, and `when_to_use`. `--pin` prints the current numbering as a paste-ready block that freezes auto-assigned keys |
| `veld runs [--name <n>] [--json]` | Run history: one row per execution instance (short id, started/ended, duration, outcome) |
| `veld runs show <id> [--json]` | One run in full: outcome, node exit codes, and the graph snapshot it was started with |
| `veld runs diff <old> <new> [--json]` | Config diff between two runs (nodes added/removed, command/cwd/env/url changes); one id diffs against its predecessor |
| `veld feedback [--name <n>]` | Open feedback UI for a run |
| `veld feedback next --wait [--name <n>]` | Block until feedback is submitted (for agent tool-use loops) |
| `veld share [RUN] [--node <n>]... [--ttl <secs>] [--approve <first\|manual\|auto>] [--web] [--access <password\|link>] [--password <pw>] [--json]` | Share a running env over an encrypted P2P tunnel; prints a join URL (and `veld join` command). `--web`: publish via the configured gateway and print public URLs (password-protected by default) |
| `veld join <TICKET> [--label <n>] [--no-remember] [--json]` | Join a shared env by ticket; materializes the shared URLs locally (blocks until approved). `--no-remember`: don't cache a relay auth token entered at the prompt |
| `veld shares [--json]` | List active shares, joins, and pending join requests; each live tunnel shows its transport (`direct`, or `relayed via <relay>` + RTT) |
| `veld approve <REQ_ID> [--json]` / `veld deny <REQ_ID> [--json]` | Resolve a pending join request |
| `veld unshare [SHARE_ID] [--json]` | Stop hosting a share (defaults to the sole active share) |
| `veld leave [JOIN_ID] [--json]` | Disconnect from a joined share (defaults to the sole active join) |
| `veld gc` | Clean up stale state and logs |
| `veld setup [unprivileged\|privileged]` | One-time system setup |
| `veld init` | Create a new veld.json (veld also reads veld.jsonc) |

All commands support `--json` for structured output, making veld scriptable and CI/agent-friendly.

---

## Architecture

Three binaries work together:

- **`veld`** — CLI. Parses commands, orchestrates environments, displays output.
- **`veld-helper`** — manages DNS entries and Caddy routes via a minimal Unix socket API. Runs as either a system daemon (privileged, for clean URLs on ports 80/443) or a user process (unprivileged, on port 18443).
- **`veld-daemon`** — user-space daemon. Monitors health, runs garbage collection, broadcasts state updates.

Caddy handles HTTPS termination and reverse proxying. Its internal CA is trusted in the system keychain during setup so browsers accept certificates without warnings.

All CLI/daemon state (run state, project registry, service logs, feedback threads and screenshots, relay auth tokens) lives in one SQLite database at `<data_dir>/veld/veld.db` (override with `VELD_DB_PATH`; `0600`, WAL mode — concurrent access without file locking). The schema is versioned and migrates forward automatically on upgrade, so a CLI update never stops running environments because the data shape changed.

An experimental second-generation management UI is served at `/ide` on the same daemon (worktree mode: import git repositories, manage `git worktree` checkouts with aliases, drive veld runs per worktree). It is also the web core of Veld Desktop, an Electron shell that wraps it.

That UI has terminal panes: real shells in the selected worktree's directory, arranged in a dock of two tab strips that can be split and rearranged. The PTY is spawned by the daemon and bridged to the browser over a WebSocket rather than run inside Electron, so terminals work in a plain browser too. Sessions outlive the page — a reload reattaches to the same shells with their scrollback, and output produced while the page was gone is replayed, so a build survives a refresh. Closing a terminal pane ends its shell; closing the window only detaches, and an abandoned session is hung up after 30 minutes. Up to 48 sessions can be live at once. Since the endpoint hands out a shell, it is gated by a single-use ticket from a CSRF-protected request plus an `Origin` allowlist, because a WebSocket handshake cannot carry the custom header the rest of the API relies on.

### Environments and runs

An **environment** is the durable named slot `--name` addresses; a **run** is one execution instance of it. Ended runs — stopped, failed, crashed, replaced, or completed (`--oneshot`) — persist as history (last 10 per environment, up to 7 days) with their logs, an explicit end reason, and machine-readable failure detail, so "why did last night's run die?" stays answerable after the fact. `veld runs` lists the history; `veld logs --run <id-prefix>` (or `-p` for the previous run) reads a past run's logs; `veld status`/`veld runs --json` expose `end_reason`/`end_detail` for agents. Crashes are detected by the daemon and recorded as `crashed` — distinguishable from a clean stop. The dashboard defaults to live environments (a top-level Active | History switcher); ended environments live under History with their last outcome, a run picker in the Logs tab, and one-click Restart. Each run also stores a **graph snapshot** taken at start — raw pre-interpolation command strings, env variable names (never values), cwd, URL templates, and a veld.json hash — so `veld runs show <id>` reconstructs what a run was started with and `veld runs diff` answers "what changed in the config between the run that worked and the run that didn't?"

---

## Feedback System

veld includes a built-in feedback overlay for human-AI collaboration. When an AI agent is iterating on UI work, humans can give structured feedback through an in-browser overlay injected into veld-served pages.

### How it works

1. When a `start_server` service is running, veld can inject a feedback overlay into the served pages
2. Humans open the feedback overlay in their browser and leave comments
3. AI agents receive the feedback via `veld feedback next --wait`, which blocks until new feedback arrives
4. The agent reads the structured feedback and iterates

### CLI Commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `veld feedback [--name <n>]` | Open feedback UI for a run |
| `veld feedback next --wait [--name <n>]` | Block until feedback is submitted (designed for agent tool-use loops) |

### Feedback API

The feedback server runs per-run and exposes:

- `POST /feedback` — Submit feedback `{ "comment": "text", "selector": "css-selector" }`
- `GET /feedback` — Get all feedback for current run
- `WS /feedback/ws` — Real-time feedback stream

The feedback overlay automatically captures React and Vue component stack traces when available, providing agents with component-level context (not just CSS selectors) for precise modifications.

The overlay survives full page reloads: when the agent's fix hot-reloads the page or the reviewer refreshes, it restores in-progress state (a half-typed element or page comment and the element it targets, the open panel/tab and scroll position, and unsent replies) from tab-local session storage — so an agent can push a fix mid-review without discarding the comment the reviewer was writing. (A screenshot comment in progress is not restored — its captured frame can't be reconstructed after a reload.)

This makes veld uniquely suited for agentic workflows where AI agents build UI and humans provide iterative feedback without context-switching.

---

## Peer-to-Peer Sharing

Share a running environment with a colleague so they open the **same** URLs on their own machine, over an encrypted peer-to-peer tunnel. No accounts, no Veld-hosted server. The tunnel uses iroh (QUIC with NAT hole-punching and an n0 relay fallback).

Services opt in explicitly: a service is shareable only if its variant declares `share.expose` in `veld.json` (`"share": { "expose": ["peer"] }`), and `veld share` refuses anything that hasn't opted in — so what leaves your machine is explicit and auditable.

### How it works

1. The host runs `veld share <run>` and gets a **join URL** to send to a colleague: `https://veld.localhost/join#<ticket>` (or `:18443` in unprivileged mode), plus a `veld join <ticket>` command as an alternative (`--json` adds a `join_url` field)
2. The colleague **opens the join URL in their browser** — it loads their own veld dashboard, which connects and waits for the host to approve (or they run `veld join <ticket>` in a terminal, which blocks until approved)
3. Once approved, veld materializes the shared URLs locally and the dashboard shows them as clickable links, so the colleague opens the same URLs the host sees
4. The consumer's own Caddy issues a locally-trusted cert, so there is no cert warning

The ticket is short and constant-size regardless of how many URLs the run exposes — the URL manifest is sent over the tunnel after approval, not embedded in the ticket.

Both people must have veld installed and be in the **same setup mode** — both privileged (clean URLs) or both unprivileged (`:18443` in URLs) — so the URLs match.

### Dashboard controls

Sharing can be driven entirely from the dashboard: each running run's card has a **Share** button; once shared it shows **Copy link** / **Copy command** buttons, an **auto-accept** toggle, and **Stop sharing**. Pending join requests (Approve/Deny) and joined shares appear in a panel.

Each run card's Services tab also shows live resource usage per node — memory and CPU summed across the node's whole process tree, refreshed every ~5s, with a memory sparkline. The same figures are available from the CLI via `veld status` (a `stats` map in `--json`).

### Security

Two gates protect every share: a capability token embedded in the ticket, plus host approval. Approval modes (`--approve`):

- **`manual`** (default for interactive use) — the host approves each join via the dashboard (which opens automatically in the browser) or `veld approve <REQ_ID>`
- **`first`** (default with `--json`) — auto-approves and pins the first token-valid joiner, rejecting the rest
- **`auto`** — approves any token-valid joiner

Traffic is end-to-end encrypted between the two velds; a relay only forwards sealed bytes and never sees URLs or content. Relay selection is a config compliance control and must be opted into explicitly — there is no implicit default, so nothing is routed over n0's public relays by accident: set `sharing.relays` in `veld.json` to `"public"` (n0's relays) or to an array of self-hosted relay URLs to keep share traffic on relays you run. `veld share` is refused if no relay is configured. n0's public relays are a free community service intended for development and testing — rate-limited, best-effort, no uptime or throughput guarantees; per [iroh's guidance](https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays) production or high-volume sharing should run on self-hosted relays. (A fair-use recommendation from n0, not a licensing restriction — iroh is dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0 and free for commercial use.) Config wins over the legacy `VELD_SHARE_RELAY` env var (read from the daemon's process environment, not your shell, and not an enforceable floor). The custom-relay guarantee covers both legs: the joining side automatically confines to the relay(s) advertised in the ticket, so a custom-relay share is never joined over n0's public relays; a joiner only sets `VELD_SHARE_RELAY` + `VELD_SHARE_RELAY_TOKEN` to supply a token for a token-gated relay. The daemon binds one iroh endpoint per relay policy on demand, so shares on different relays (e.g. public and a self-hosted relay) run concurrently without conflict. A self-hosted relay can require an authorization token so it isn't an open relay: write a relay entry as `{ "url": ..., "token": ... }` and Veld sends the token as an `Authorization: Bearer` header. The token is a literal string, or — to keep the secret out of `veld.json` — `{ "env": "VAR" }`, `{ "file": "/run/secrets/…" }` (Docker/K8s mounts), or `{ "shell": "op read op://vault/relay/token" }` (secret-manager CLI; runs with the user's login-shell PATH, so `op` etc. are found even though the daemon has a bare service PATH); it is resolved on the daemon at share time, and a token that fails to resolve fails the share rather than connecting unauthenticated. On the join side, a token-gated relay prompts the joiner for the token (browser overlay or `veld join` terminal), caches it per relay in the central veld database (`<data_dir>/veld/veld.db`, 0600) so future joins don't re-ask, and re-prompts on a wrong token; the token can also come from `VELD_SHARE_RELAY` + `VELD_SHARE_RELAY_TOKEN` (attached only to the matching ticket relay), or the host sets `sharing.dangerouslyEmbedRelayTokensInTicket: true` to embed the token in the ticket so joiners need no setup — dangerous, since the relay secret then rides in every share link, so disposable per-project tokens only.

### Public web sharing

`share.expose` also accepts `web`: expose a service to anyone with a browser — no Veld on the viewer's side — via a self-hosted gateway. Configure `sharing.gateway` (a URL, or `{ "url": ..., "token": ... }` where `token` is a secret source like relay tokens; the gateway requires registration auth) and run `veld share --web`. This mints a **separate** share scoped to the `web`-opted services (own capability — revoking web never touches peer shares), registers it with the gateway, and prints real public URLs of the form `https://<slug>.<gateway-domain>`. Slugs are deterministic (a hash bound to the sharing machine, service, and share capability — stable across gateway restarts) and unguessable. **Web shares are password-protected by default**: `veld share --web` generates and prints a viewer password (`--password` to choose it); the gateway shows a password page, then a per-slug session cookie (12 h, capped at the share TTL, stateless — signed with a capability-derived key, so gateway restarts don't log viewers out) keeps the viewer in. The printed one-link (`https://…/#veld-key=…`) carries the password in the URL fragment, which never reaches DNS, TLS, or server logs. Opt a service out with `"share": { "expose": ["web"], "web": { "access": "link" } }` (or `--access link` for config-silent services; explicit config wins) — then the unguessable slug is the only gate and the link must be treated as a secret. Multi-service caveat: the session cookie is per public host, so give a password-protected frontend's API nodes `"web": { "access": "link" }` or cross-origin fetches get 401s. Web shares default to a 3600s TTL (peer: 7200s). The daemon heartbeats the registration; `veld unshare` or the TTL kills the URLs. WebSockets/HMR work through the gateway; the app sees its own origin hostname in `Host` (dev-server allow-lists pass) and, in lockstep, the same host in `Origin`/`Referer` on every request including WebSocket upgrades — so a dev server that gates HMR on `Origin` (Next.js) needs its origin host in the framework's `allowedDevOrigins`, or the service's `proxy.request.remove: ["Origin"]` opt-in to drop the header. The public host arrives in `X-Forwarded-Host`, redirects between shared services are rewritten to public URLs, and origin-scoped cookie domains are made host-only. Hard-coded absolute URLs, CORS allow-lists, and OAuth redirect URIs are the operator's domain setup — Veld never rewrites bodies. The toolbar's arc menu has a top-level **Sharing** item (marked with a dot when the page is web-shared) whose submenu covers **Start/Stop sharing** (toggle a web share for the page's run from the browser), **Copy public URL** (turns the current page into its public deep link, path + query + hash preserved), and **Sharing status**. Transport detail is not shown in the toolbar — `veld shares` prints each live tunnel's transport: `direct` (full bandwidth) or `relayed via <relay>` (throughput capped by that relay — the usual cause of slow shares), and the management UI shows the same. The gateway itself (`veld-gateway`) is one stateless container: `ghcr.io/prosperity-solutions/veld-gateway`, configured entirely via env vars (`VELD_GATEWAY_DOMAIN`, `VELD_GATEWAY_TOKEN`, `VELD_GATEWAY_RELAYS`, …), needing a wildcard DNS record plus TLS (built-in cert files or an external L7 terminator).

### Behavior

- **Collision** — if the consumer already runs the same environment, the local URL wins: that node is skipped and reported as a warning
- **Fail-closed** — shares are held in the daemon's memory; if the daemon stops, shares stop
- **Auto-teardown** — stopping the run (`veld stop`) auto-unshares its shares, and so do `veld restart` and a `veld start` that replaces a live same-named environment (each mints a new run, so the old share would point at torn-down ports); a share whose run ended some other way (a crash) is listed as a "share without a run" in the dashboard with an Unshare button; a consumer's join self-tears-down when the tunnel closes
- **Optional ids** — `veld unshare` and `veld leave` take the id optionally, resolving the sole active share/join when omitted
- **TTL** — shares expire after `--ttl` seconds (default 7200)

### CLI Commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `veld share [RUN] [--node <n>]... [--ttl <secs>] [--approve <first\|manual\|auto>] [--web] [--access <password\|link>] [--password <pw>] [--json]` | Start sharing a running env; prints a join URL (and `veld join` command). `--web`: publish the `web`-opted services via the configured gateway and print public URLs (password-protected by default) |
| `veld join <TICKET> [--label <n>] [--no-remember] [--json]` | Join a shared env by ticket (blocks until approved). `--no-remember`: don't cache a prompted relay auth token |
| `veld shares [--json]` | List active shares, joins, and pending join requests; each live tunnel shows its transport (`direct`, or `relayed via <relay>` + RTT) |
| `veld approve <REQ_ID> [--json]` / `veld deny <REQ_ID> [--json]` | Resolve a pending join request |
| `veld unshare [SHARE_ID] [--json]` | Stop hosting a share (defaults to the sole active share) |
| `veld leave [JOIN_ID] [--json]` | Disconnect from a joined share (defaults to the sole active join) |

---

## Client-Side Log Collection

Veld automatically captures browser console output from `start_server` nodes. A small script is injected into proxied HTML responses that hooks `console.log`, `console.warn`, `console.error`, `console.info`, and `console.debug`, plus `window.onerror` and `onunhandledrejection`.

Captured logs appear alongside server logs in `veld logs` and the management UI. Filter by source:

```sh
veld logs --source client          # Browser logs only
veld logs --source server          # Server logs only
veld logs --source internal        # Liveness probe & recovery logs
veld logs --source all             # All sources (default)
```

### Configuration

Control which levels to capture with `client_log_levels` at the project, node, or variant level (most specific wins):

```json
"client_log_levels": ["log", "warn", "error", "info", "debug"]
```

Valid levels: `"log"`, `"warn"`, `"error"`, `"info"`, `"debug"`. Default: `["log", "warn", "error"]`. Unhandled exceptions and promise rejections are always captured regardless of this setting.

The management UI also provides source filter controls (All / Server / Client) in the Logs tab.

### Feature Toggles

Control which Veld capabilities are injected into `start_server` nodes' HTML responses with `features` at the project, node, or variant level (most specific wins):

```json
"features": { "feedback_overlay": false, "client_logs": true }
```

Available features: `feedback_overlay` (toolbar/comments UI), `client_logs` (browser log collector), `inject` (auto-inject bootstrap scripts). All default to `true`.

### Proxy Header Rules

Rewrite headers on the way through the reverse proxies with `proxy` at the project, node, or variant level (most specific wins; `remove` lists union, `set` maps merge per key). Applies to both the local Caddy proxy and the public web gateway (`veld share --web`); it does not apply to direct iroh peer sharing, which is a transport-level byte splice with no HTTP layer.

```json
"proxy": {
  "request":  { "remove": ["Origin"], "set": { "X-Env": "dev" } },
  "response": { "set": { "X-Frame-Options": "DENY" } }
}
```

`request` rules apply to the upstream request, `response` rules to the returned response; `remove` strips header names, `set` overwrites them (names matched case-insensitively). By default Veld does no header manipulation: `Origin` passes through the local proxy, and the gateway rewrites it coherently to the origin host on every request (including WebSocket upgrades) rather than dropping it. A dev server that gates WS HMR on `Origin` (Next.js) should list its origin host in the framework's own `allowedDevOrigins`; where no allow-list exists, `proxy.request.remove: ["Origin"]` drops the header entirely.

---

## Configuration Reference

### Top-Level Structure

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `$schema` | string | No | JSON Schema URL for editor autocompletion |
| `schemaVersion` | string | Yes (root file only) | Must be `"3"`. `"1"` and `"2"` are not supported and fail to load with a message stating every change needed. veld ships no converter — `docs/migrating-to-v3.md` is the rule set, `veld lint` is the check |
| `include` | string[] | No | v3: globs of further config files, relative to the root file. Splits a large config across per-directory files. A node is defined in exactly one file |
| `vars` | object | No | v3: one definition point per value, referenced as `${vars.name}`. A scalar or a single value source — never a config fragment |
| `name` | string | Yes | Project name (used in URLs) |
| `url_template` | string | No | URL template for services |
| `presets` | object | No | Named shortcuts for node:variant selections |
| `default_preset` | string | No | Preset used when `veld start` is given nothing. Must name a defined preset |
| `client_log_levels` | array | No | Browser log levels to capture (default: `["log", "warn", "error"]`) |
| `features` | object | No | Feature toggles: `feedback_overlay`, `client_logs`, `inject` (all default `true`, cascade: variant > node > project) |
| `proxy` | object | No | Reverse-proxy header rules (`request`/`response`, each with `remove`/`set`); applies to the local proxy + web gateway (cascade: variant > node > project; `remove` unions, `set` merges) |
| `env` | object | No | Global environment variables inherited by all nodes (cascade: variant > node > project, per-key merge) |
| `setup` | array | No | Lifecycle steps before graph execution (see Setup & Teardown) |
| `teardown` | array | No | Lifecycle steps after all nodes stop (see Setup & Teardown) |
| `nodes` | object | Yes | The dependency graph nodes |

### Setup & Teardown

Project-level lifecycle steps that run outside the dependency graph. Not nodes — no variants, no health checks, no outputs.

**Setup** runs sequentially before any node. Non-zero exit aborts startup. **Teardown** runs after all nodes stop (after per-node `on_stop` hooks). Best-effort.

```json
"setup": [
  { "name": "docker", "shell": "docker info", "failureMessage": "Docker must be running" },
  { "name": "network", "shell": "docker network create ${veld.name}-net 2>/dev/null || true" }
],
"teardown": [
  { "name": "network", "shell": "docker network rm ${veld.name}-net 2>/dev/null || true" }
]
```

Step fields: `name` (required), `argv` or `shell` (required, exactly one), `failureMessage` (optional — shown on failure).

Variables: `${veld.name}`, `${veld.project}`, `${veld.root}`, `${veld.run}`, `${veld.worktree}`, `${veld.branch}`, `${veld.username}` and `${vars.*}`, plus shell env vars. No node-scoped vars (`${veld.port}`, `${veld.url}`, `${veld.node}`, `${nodes.*}`) and no `${veld.run_id}` — a teardown step also runs from `veld stop` after the run row is gone.

### Step Types

#### `start_server`

Starts and manages a long-lived process. Veld allocates a port, injects it as `${veld.port}`, configures DNS and Caddy routing, and monitors health.

- Must specify exactly one of `argv` (array, spawned directly) or `shell` (string, via `sh -c`)
- The process must bind to `${veld.port}`
- Built-in outputs: `url` (full HTTPS URL) and `port` (allocated port number)
- Supports synthetic `outputs` as an object (key → template string, interpolated after port allocation)
- Requires `health_check`

```json
{
  "type": "start_server",
  "shell": "npm run dev -- --port ${veld.port}",
  "health_check": { "type": "http", "path": "/health" }
}
```

#### `command`

Runs a shell command or script to completion. Used for setup tasks.

- Must specify either `command` or `script` (mutually exclusive)
- Can emit outputs by writing `key=value` lines to `$VELD_OUTPUT_FILE` (preferred) or via `VELD_OUTPUT key=value` on stdout (legacy, discouraged)
- Declares outputs as an array of strings
- Built-in output: `exit_code`
- Supports `skip_if` for idempotency (alias: `verify`)
- Does NOT get a port allocated — `${veld.port}` is not available

```json
{
  "type": "command",
  "script": "./scripts/clone-db.sh",
  "outputs": ["DATABASE_URL"]
}
```

### Health Checks

Two-phase: (1) TCP port check, (2) HTTP endpoint check. Three strategies:

```json
{ "type": "http", "path": "/health", "expect_status": 200, "timeout_seconds": 30 }
{ "type": "port", "timeout_seconds": 10 }
{ "type": "command", "shell": "curl -sf http://localhost:${veld.port}/ready" }
```

### Dependencies

Dependencies are explicit `node:variant` pairs. Resolved before start. Started in topological order, parallelized where possible. Reverse-order teardown.

```json
"depends_on": {
  "database": "docker",
  "backend": "local"
}
```

### Environment Variables

Declare `env` at the project, node, or variant level. Variables cascade: variant > node > project (per-key merge, most specific wins). Values support variable interpolation including upstream node outputs:

```json
{
  "env": { "SHARED_FLAG": "1" },
  "nodes": {
    "api": {
      "env": { "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" },
      "variants": {
        "local": {
          "env": {
            "DATABASE_URL": "${nodes.database.DATABASE_URL}",
            "PORT": "${veld.port}",
            "NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL": "${nodes.backend.url}"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Outputs

For `start_server` variants — object (synthetic templates):
```json
"outputs": {
  "DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://postgres:veld@localhost:${veld.port}/app"
}
```

For `command` variants — array (captured from `$VELD_OUTPUT_FILE` or legacy `VELD_OUTPUT` stdout):
```json
"outputs": ["DATABASE_URL", "DB_NAME"]
```

### Variable Substitution

#### Built-in Variables (`${veld.*}`)

| Variable | Value |
|----------|-------|
| `${veld.port}` | Allocated port (start_server only) |
| `${veld.url}` | Full HTTPS URL (start_server only) |
| `${veld.url.hostname}` | DNS name only (e.g. `app.my-run.proj.localhost`) |
| `${veld.url.host}` | hostname:port (omits port if 443) |
| `${veld.url.origin}` | scheme + host (same as `${veld.url}`) |
| `${veld.url.scheme}` | Protocol scheme (`https`) |
| `${veld.url.port}` | HTTPS port (`${veld.port}` is the backend bind port) |
| `${veld.run}` | Run name |
| `${veld.run_id}` | Stable run UUID |
| `${veld.root}` | Path to the directory containing the root config |
| `${veld.project}` | Project name |
| `${veld.name}` | Project name (alias for `${veld.project}`) |
| `${veld.worktree}` | Slugified worktree directory name |
| `${veld.branch}` | Current git branch (slugified) |
| `${veld.username}` | OS username |
| `${veld.node}` | This node's name |
| `${veld.variant}` | This variant's name |
| `${veld.ports.<name>}` | A named port from this node's `ports` map (start_server only) |

Availability is not uniform, and `veld lint` checks a reference against the context it sits in
(`builtin-not-in-scope`): `port`/`url`/`url.*`/`ports.*` exist only on a `start_server` node,
`node`/`variant` only on a node, `run_id` not in a project `setup`/`teardown` step, and a `vars`
value gets the run-scoped names only (a var is one value for the whole run, so compose per-node
ones at the use site). A node's `on_stop` receives exactly what the node had, URL family included.

#### Node Output References (`${nodes.*}`)

```
${nodes.database.DATABASE_URL}   # custom output
${nodes.backend.url}             # start_server built-in: HTTPS URL
${nodes.backend.url.hostname}    # start_server built-in: DNS name only
${nodes.backend.url.host}        # start_server built-in: hostname:port
${nodes.backend.url.origin}      # start_server built-in: scheme + host
${nodes.backend.url.scheme}      # start_server built-in: protocol scheme
${nodes.backend.url.port}        # start_server built-in: HTTPS port
${nodes.backend.port}            # start_server built-in: backend bind port
${nodes.backend:local.url}       # qualified form (when multiple variants active)
```

### URL Templates

URL templates use `{variable}` syntax (single braces). Available variables:

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `{service}` | Node name |
| `{variant}` | Variant name |
| `{run}` | Run name (always non-empty) |
| `{project}` | Project name |
| `{branch}` | Git branch (slugified) |
| `{worktree}` | Worktree directory name (slugified) |
| `{username}` | OS username |
| `{hostname}` | Machine hostname |

Fallback operator: `{branch ?? run}` uses first non-empty value.

Default: `{service}.{run}.{project}.localhost`

`.localhost` resolves to 127.0.0.1 automatically (RFC 6761). Custom domains are supported in privileged mode only — veld manages exact DNS entries via veld-helper (requires `/etc/hosts` or dnsmasq access). In unprivileged/auto mode, `veld start` will refuse to start if any URL template resolves to a non-`.localhost` domain.

### URL Template Cascade

1. Variant-level (highest priority)
2. Node-level
3. Project-level (default)

### Presets

Named shortcuts for node:variant selections. A preset is either a bare list of
selections, or an object adding a stable picker key and the metadata needed to
choose it. Both forms are fully supported.

```jsonc
"presets": {
  // List form.
  "fullstack": ["database:docker", "backend:local", "frontend:local"],
  "frontend-only": ["frontend:local"],

  // Object form.
  "designer-preview": {
    "key": 1,
    "label": "Site preview (staging content)",
    "when_to_use": "Reviewing visual changes against real CMS content. Slow to start; not for API work.",
    "group": "For non-developers",
    "selections": ["frontend:prod", "backend:staging"]
  }
},
"default_preset": "fullstack"
```

Usage: `veld start --preset fullstack --name my-feature`, or `veld start --preset 1`.
In a script, pass the name or a pinned key — an unpinned key can move.

Upgrading from an earlier veld: the picker's numbers used to be positions in an
alphabetically sorted list and are now assigned in declaration order, so they change
once. Re-check any runbook naming a number, then `veld presets --pin` to freeze them.

**`key` is an identity, not a list position.** A pinned key does not move when
presets are added, removed, renamed, or regrouped, so the number someone
memorised stays correct. Presets without a key take the lowest unclaimed number in
declaration order: appending a preset changes no existing key, and neither does
pinning one at the number it already shows. An unpinned key does move when a
preset is added or removed ahead of it in declaration order — including from
another `include` file that sorts earlier. `veld presets` marks the auto-assigned
keys; `veld presets --pin` prints a block to paste that freezes them (veld never
rewrites a config itself).

`label`, `when_to_use`, and `group` are what make a long preset list pickable by
someone who did not write it — and by a coding agent, which reads `when_to_use`
from `veld presets` / `veld presets --json` to decide what to start. Groups are
ordered by their lowest member key, so a group can move on screen without changing
a number; the list is ascending within a group rather than globally. Ungrouped
presets are collected under `Other`.

`default_preset` is what `veld start` uses when given nothing: enter at the
picker, and without a TTY it is used directly instead of failing with "No
selections provided".

### Additional Variant Fields

| Field | Type | Applies To | Description |
|-------|------|------------|-------------|
| `argv` / `shell` | array / string | All | What to run — exactly one. `argv` is spawned directly (no shell, no word splitting); `shell` runs via `sh -c`. Interpolation in an `argv` runs per element after the array is fixed, so a value containing spaces can never change the argument count |
| `on_stop` | object | All | Teardown command (`{"argv": …}` / `{"shell": …}`) on `veld stop`. Declarable at node level; a variant erases an inherited hook with `"on_stop": null` |
| `skip_if` | object | `command` only | Idempotency check (exit 0 = skip), as `{"argv": …}` / `{"shell": …}`. Alias: `verify` |
| `probes` | object | All | `{readiness?: HealthCheck, liveness?: LivenessProbe}` — supersedes `health_check` |
| `sensitive_outputs` | array | All | Output keys to mask and encrypt |
| `client_log_levels` | array | `start_server` | Browser log levels override (variant > node > project) |
| `features` | object | `start_server` | Feature toggles override (variant > node > project) |
| `proxy` | object | `start_server` | Reverse-proxy header rules override (variant > node > project; `remove` unions, `set` merges) |
| `cwd` | string | All | Working directory (relative paths resolve from project root). Cascade: variant > node. Supports `${...}` substitution. |
| `hidden` (node-level) | boolean | All | Hide from `veld nodes` output |

---

## Complete Example

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://veld.oss.life.li/schema/v3/veld.schema.json",
  "schemaVersion": "3",
  "name": "myproject",
  "url_template": "{service}.{run}.myproject.localhost",
  "presets": {
    "fullstack": ["database:docker", "backend:local", "frontend:local"],
    "frontend-only": ["frontend:local"]
  },
  "nodes": {
    "database": {
      "default_variant": "docker",
      "variants": {
        "docker": {
          "type": "start_server",
          "shell": "docker run --rm -p ${veld.port}:5432 postgres:16",
          "health_check": { "type": "port", "timeout_seconds": 15 },
          "outputs": {
            "DATABASE_URL": "postgres://dev:dev@localhost:${veld.port}/app"
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "backend": {
      "default_variant": "local",
      "variants": {
        "local": {
          "type": "start_server",
          "shell": "cargo run -- --port ${veld.port}",
          "health_check": { "type": "http", "path": "/health" },
          "depends_on": { "database": "docker" },
          "env": {
            "DATABASE_URL": "${nodes.database.DATABASE_URL}"
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "frontend": {
      "default_variant": "local",
      "variants": {
        "local": {
          "type": "start_server",
          "shell": "npm run dev -- --port ${veld.port}",
          "health_check": { "type": "http", "path": "/" },
          "depends_on": { "backend": "local" },
          "env": {
            "API_URL": "${nodes.backend.url}"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

## Agent Skills

Veld ships skills for AI coding agents. Install them so your agent knows how to configure, use, and collaborate through Veld:

```sh
npx skills add prosperity-solutions/veld
```

This installs three skills:

- **veld-config** — Write and edit `veld.json` configuration files (nodes, health checks, dependencies, URL templates, presets)
- **veld-feedback** — Human-in-the-loop feedback workflow (request reviews, read structured comments with element selectors and component traces, iterate)
- **veld-usage** — CLI reference for agents (start, stop, logs, status, feedback, and all other commands)

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, Cline, GitHub Copilot, and [40+ more agents](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills#supported-agents).

---

## Requirements

- macOS (arm64/x64) or Linux (x64/arm64)
- Optional: sudo access for `veld setup privileged` (clean URLs without port numbers, custom apex domains)
